The bounty named is explained as the bounty of repentance. Allah granted it to them after their turning away, so the sentence states that the punishment was withheld for a reason that came from Him and not from them.

The address itself is then discussed. It is directed to the People of the Book who were living in the place to which the Messenger of Allah had emigrated, in his days, even though the deed spoken of was done by their forefathers. Some have claimed that the address is delivered this way only by ascribing the deed to those being addressed while the deed belonged in reality to others, because the people addressed are the descendants of those who did it.

phrases.translation: you would have certainly been of the losers
phrases.ar: لَكُنتُم مِّنَ ٱلۡخَٰسِرِينَ
phrases.explanation: The consequence is stated in the same terms as the bounty before it. Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon them and His mercy toward them, by saving them through the acceptance of their repentance for their sin and their crime, they would have been among the losers. The saving is therefore located in the acceptance of repentance, and the loss they escaped is the loss of people whose sin stands against them with no way back.

phrases.translation: You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath.
phrases.ar: وَلَقَدۡ عَلِمۡتُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱعۡتَدَوۡاْ مِنكُمۡ فِي ٱلسَّبۡتِ
phrases.explanation:
Knowing is explained first as coming to know, and the ordinary saying is quoted as a parallel, so the verse addresses people who have this knowledge and not people who must be told it for the first time.

The verse is then placed. It and the verses after it enumerate for the children of Israel who were dwelling among the people of the Prophet what their forefathers did, which is why a story from the past is told as a matter the listeners already know.

The Sabbath is explained from its root. Its origin is rest and stillness in repose and ease, and for that reason the sleeper is described by a word from the same root, because of his rest and the stillness of his body and his repose. What was transgressed was therefore a day defined by leaving work alone, and the transgression lay in doing on it what the day required them not to do.

phrases.translation: We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”
phrases.ar: فَقُلۡنَا لَهُمۡ كُونُواْ قِرَدَةً خَٰسِـِٔينَ
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained as addressed to those who transgressed concerning the Sabbath, and the two words joined in it are taken together. Being made apes is the change of form, and the word translated as disgraced is explained as being removed from the good and made humbled and lowly.

A dissenting statement is then rejected. What Mujahid said is judged to contradict the plain meaning to which the Book of Allah points, because Allah reported in His Book what He did to them, and it is noted in addition that this statement contradicts the totality of the authoritative tradition, in which error and falsehood are impossible.

phrases.translation: So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing
phrases.ar: فَجَعَلۡنَٰهَا نَكَٰلٗا لِّمَا بَيۡنَ يَدَيۡهَا وَمَا خَلۡفَهَا وَمَوۡعِظَةٗ لِّلۡمُتَّقِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse turns on a pronoun, and the scholars of exegesis differ over what it refers back to in the words We made it. Two sayings are recorded first, and then two more.

On the saying reported from Ibn Abbas the pronoun refers to the transformation of form, which is a verbal noun on a known pattern, since Allah transformed their form by it. The meaning of the words on this interpretation is then spelled out. We said to them, be despised apes, and they became apes transformed in form, and We made Our punishment of them and Our transformation of them into what the verse goes on to describe.

On the second saying the pronoun refers to the fish, even though no prior mention of them had been made, because there was in the report an indication of them and so reference could be made to them. On the third it refers to the town whose inhabitants transgressed the Sabbath, so the sense is that We made that town a deterring example. On the fourth it refers to the apes who had been transformed in form, and the sense is that We made them a deterring example for those who preceded them and those who came after.

The sayings are then weighed. The interpretation that takes the pronoun as the fish is judged the furthest of them, since deriving that sense is more remote than the others, and a note is added on the reading that takes what precedes and what follows as towns rather than as times.

The interpretation given is the one that follows from what was set out before. We said to them, be despised apes, and We made Our punishment of them a punishment for the sins that preceded it and for what followed, and We made it a deterring example for those who came after and a reminder for the God-fearing so that they would be admonished by it. Allah therefore made the punishment He sent down on those who transgressed the Sabbath into an admonition specifically for the God-fearing and a warning example for the believers, which is why the verse ends on them rather than on the people punished.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوۡمِهِۦٓ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأۡمُرُكُمۡ أَن تَذۡبَحُواْ بَقَرَةٗۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُوٗاۖ قَالَ أَعُوذُ بِٱللَّهِ أَنۡ أَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The command to slaughter a cow is explained together with the answer it drew. When they said to Moses what they said, he told them that whoever reports on behalf of Allah, whether a command or a prohibition, does not make a jest of it, and it is not fitting for the prophets of Allah that they should mock in anything they carry from Him. His seeking refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant is therefore read as a denial that he was joking, since joking about what Allah commands is itself ignorance.

The occasion of the command is then given. The reports all mention the reason for which Moses said to them that Allah commands them to slaughter a cow, and it concerns a killing that had taken place among them and their dispute about who was responsible for it. The people to whom the command was addressed are identified with that occasion in view, which is why a command that sounds unconnected to what came before it is in fact the way out of a quarrel they could not settle.

phrases.translation: They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!”
phrases.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَۚ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةٞ لَّا فَارِضٞ وَلَا بِكۡرٌ عَوَانُۢ بَيۡنَ ذَٰلِكَۖ
phrases.explanation:
The question they asked is reported first, that he call on his Lord for them so that He makes clear to them what she is, and the answer describes the cow by her age.

The three terms used are explained in order. The word for old is taken in that sense, and in accordance with this explanation the commentators spoke, with the reports naming who said it recorded. The word for young is explained as the female of livestock, and among the children of Adam the one that the male has not yet come to, so it names an animal that has not been bred from. The third word means of middle age, and it is placed between the two, which is what the answer says in words, neither old nor young but in between.

The larger question raised by these verses is then discussed at length, namely whether their repeated asking was itself a fault. The statements reported from the Companions and the Successors and those who followed them are set out, and all whose statements are mentioned held the questioning of their prophet about the attributes of the cow to be blameworthy. They were of the view that when the people asked about her age and he told them, restricting them to one age rather than another and one kind rather than another, it became obligatory on them to slaughter any cow answering that description.

The same reasoning is applied to the second situation, where they were of the view that it was obligatory on them to apply the outward import of the command and slaughter any animal they wished to which the description applied, and likewise to the third matter, in which they were in the same condition as in the first and the second. On this reading each answer narrowed what they had to find, and each further question narrowed it again against their own interest.

A contrary claim is recorded and rejected. Some whose ignorance was great and whose confusion was severe claimed that the people asked Moses what they asked only after Allah had commanded them to slaughter a cow among particular cows. It is answered that had such a person reflected on his own statement, what appeared difficult to him would have become easy, since he found it astonishing that the people should ask about a matter they had already been given in full.

phrases.translation: He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”
phrases.ar: فَٱفۡعَلُواْ مَا تُؤۡمَرُونَ
phrases.explanation: The closing command is explained as an instruction to stop asking and to act. Allah says to them, do what I command you, and then you will attain your needs and your requests, so obedience is placed before the satisfaction of what they were asking for and not after it.

phrases.translation: They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.”
phrases.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا لَوۡنُهَاۚ
phrases.explanation: The second question is reported in the same words as the first, that he call on his Lord for them so that He makes clear to them what her color is. The meaning of the request is then explained, that they were asking what thing her color is, and a point of grammar follows from that reading, since the word for color stands in the nominative because the question is framed as what is her color rather than as a description to be supplied.

phrases.translation: He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”
phrases.ar: قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةٞ صَفۡرَآءُ فَاقِعٞ لَّوۡنُهَا تَسُرُّ ٱلنَّٰظِرِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The answer is explained word by word. The color named is discussed by the exegetes, who differed about it, some taking it in one sense and others saying that it means yellow of horn and hoof, and the reports of who said each are given. A witness from the language is examined, in which camels described by the word for yellow are in fact black, and it is answered that even if camels are described in that way it does not belong to the way cows are described, since the Arabs do not describe them by that word in the same sense.

The word that intensifies the color is then explained as meaning pure of color, and it is noted that this intensifying form with yellow is the counterpart of the form used with white, so each color has its own word for being unmixed. The closing phrase is explained as meaning that this cow gladdens those who look at her, in the beauty of her form and her appearance, which completes the description by adding what the eye takes from it.

phrases.translation: Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow,
phrases.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَ
phrases.explanation:
The third question is reported, and the people who asked it are identified as the people of Moses, those who had been commanded to slaughter the cow, speaking to Moses himself. His name is left out of the sentence while the pronoun refers back to him, which is noted as a feature of the wording.

The question is then read as a statement about them rather than a simple request. It is an announcement from Allah about the people concerning a third instance of ignorance on their part, for if they had been given what they needed at the first command they would not have come back to ask twice more. The pattern is drawn out, that when the people went on causing their prophet more vexation and obstinacy, Allah increased for them the narrowing of what they had to find, so each question made the matter harder for the people who asked it.

phrases.translation: for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”
phrases.ar: إِنَّ ٱلۡبَقَرَ تَشَٰبَهَ عَلَيۡنَا وَإِنَّآ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَمُهۡتَدُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The complaint that the cows are confused to them is discussed in the recitation first. Some recited it with a form that announces about the masculine, for the reason given earlier in a parallel reading, and the correct view about the reading is stated, that it is recited with the lightening of one letter and a particular vowel on another, so the word is read as a plain statement that the cows have become alike to them.

Their closing words are then explained. If Allah wills, we will be guided means that they will come to perceive what they had been unable to distinguish, so the guidance asked for is guidance to the right animal, and it is tied to the will of Allah rather than to another round of questions.

phrases.translation: He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’”
phrases.ar: قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةٞ لَّا ذَلُولٞ تُثِيرُ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ وَلَا تَسۡقِي ٱلۡحَرۡثَ مُسَلَّمَةٞ لَّا شِيَةَ فِيهَاۚ
phrases.explanation:
The answer is explained term by term. Moses says that Allah describes the cow they are commanded to slaughter, and the first of the descriptions is that labor has not made it submissive, so it is an animal not worn out by work. The clause about ploughing is then explained as turning the earth over for cultivation, with the ordinary use of the verb in Arabic given, and the clause about watering the tilth as drawing water for the crops.

The word translated as wholesome is explained from its form. It is a passive derivation from the word for soundness, and the ordinary saying built on the same root is quoted. Others took it to mean made free of defects, and the reports naming who said that are given with it.

The last description is treated at length. No marking upon it means that there is no color on the animal differing from the color of its hide. The word is traced to its origin, which is the adorning of a garment, that is, embellishing its unevenness with various colors in its warp and its weft, and the verb for adorning a garment is quoted in its forms. From the same root comes the word for an informer, so called because he lies about a man to a ruler and embellishes his lie with falsehoods, and the verbal noun for informing is given with a line of poetry as its witness.

Two explanations of these terms are then weighed. What Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Aliya and those who said the same as them said is judged more fitting for the verse than what Mujahid said. The reason is that if soundness had concerned the kinds of color other than the color of the hide, the word for wholesome would already have been a sufficient statement and would have made the words no marking upon it superfluous. Since those words are there, they make clear that wholesome means something other than what they mean, so the two descriptions are read as covering soundness from defects on the one hand and evenness of color on the other.

phrases.translation: They said, “Now you have come with the truth.”
phrases.ar: قَالُواْ ٱلۡـَٰٔنَ جِئۡتَ بِٱلۡحَقِّۚ
phrases.explanation: The words they answered with are reported, and a claim made about them is recorded. Some of the predecessors held that the people apostatized from their religion and became unbelievers by saying now you have come with the truth, as though what had been given to them before was not the truth. The saying is read on its face as an admission that the description is now complete, so that nothing is left for them to ask about, and the verse moves at once to what they did with it.

phrases.translation: Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly
phrases.ar: فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُواْ يَفۡعَلُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The slaughter is explained first as a plain fact. The people of Moses slaughtered the cow that Allah had commanded them to slaughter, so after all the questioning the command was carried out.

The clause saying that they almost did not is then discussed. The exegetes differed about the reason why they came close to leaving the duty Allah had imposed on them, and the reports naming who gave each reason are recorded. One reason given is that they were almost brought to not doing it out of fear of disgrace, should Allah reveal through it the murderer of the slain man. The hesitation named in the verse is therefore traced to something other than reluctance to pay for the animal, and the two accounts are left side by side.

phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was,
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قَتَلۡتُمۡ نَفۡسٗا فَٱدَّٰرَٰءۡتُمۡ فِيهَاۖ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as a reminder. By the words and when you killed a soul, Allah means, remember when you killed a soul, and the address runs to the children of Israel for what their forefathers did.

The dispute named after it is explained from the verb. Its sense is given as going against one another, and the ordinary saying is quoted in which a person does not dispute with his companion and business partner. It was also said that the meaning here is that they repelled one another about it, each pushing the charge onto another, which is the shape a murder takes when no one admits to it.

Their mutual difference, dispute and quarrel is then described as concerning the affair of the slain man whose matter has been mentioned, so the verse returns to the killing that the whole passage about the cow was sent down for.

phrases.translation: but Allah revealed what you concealed
phrases.ar: وَٱللَّهُ مُخۡرِجٞ مَّا كُنتُمۡ تَكۡتُمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Bringing out is explained from its sense in this place. It means making visible and manifest to the one from whom a thing was hidden, so what Allah does here is not a new act of knowledge but an act of disclosure.

What was concealed and then brought out is named. It is the killing done by the killer of the slain man, and that killer had concealed his deed from the people among whom the dispute ran. The disclosure is therefore the answer to the quarrel described in the first part of the verse, and it is what the command about the cow was for.

phrases.translation: So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.”
phrases.ar: فَقُلۡنَا ٱضۡرِبُوهُ بِبَعۡضِهَاۚ
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained first. By the words then We said, strike him with part of her, Allah means that He said to the people of Moses, those who had disputed over the slain man, that they should strike him with a part of the cow they had been made to describe in such detail.

The scholars then differed about which part of the cow the slain man was struck with, and which bodily part of it that was. Several answers are recorded, one after another, with the reports naming who said each of them, and one of the answers given is that he was struck with the piece of flesh between the two shoulder blades.

A question is raised about the command itself. Where is the report showing that Allah commanded them this for that purpose, since the verse does not state the purpose in words? The answer is given at length, and it turns on the fact that the command and the killing it answers are joined in the passage itself, so the purpose is known from the sequence of the verses rather than from a separate report.

phrases.translation: This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life,
phrases.ar: كَذَٰلِكَ يُحۡيِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰ
phrases.explanation:
The clause that follows is explained as an address from Allah to those who saw what happened, and its sense is that this is how Allah brings the dead to life. One dead man restored in front of witnesses is put forward as a sample of what He does on a larger scale.

It is also noted that Allah adduced this as a proof against the polytheists among the Arabs, even though the event belonged to another people, since a proof of this kind does not depend on who watched it happen first.

phrases.translation: showing you His signs so that you may understand
phrases.ar: وَيُرِيكُمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَعۡقِلُونَ
phrases.explanation: The closing clause is explained as an address to those who deny the Resurrection. Allah shows them His signs so that they may understand, and the signs named here are the ones just described, the dead man brought back and the cow whose description was given in such detail that no one could mistake which animal was meant.

phrases.translation: Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder,
phrases.ar: ثُمَّ قَسَتۡ قُلُوبُكُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ ذَٰلِكَ فَهِيَ كَٱلۡحِجَارَةِ أَوۡ أَشَدُّ قَسۡوَةٗۚ
phrases.explanation:
The hardening is placed in time first. After all that means after Allah brought to life for them the murdered man about whose death they had disputed, so what follows a sign they saw with their own eyes is described as a hardening of the heart rather than a lack of evidence.

The comparison is then explained. The word translated as they refers to their hearts, and the sense given is that their hearts hardened after they had seen what they saw, until they became like stones or harder still. The two degrees are named in one breath, which raises a question.

A questioner asks what the explanation of like stones or even harder is, since the wording appears to leave it open which of the two their hearts resemble. The answer is that it is not as the questioner imagined, and that the wording is not a doubt on Allah's part about which of the two is the case. The comparison is put to the one who hears it, so the listener is told that those hearts reached at least the hardness of stone, and that they may have gone past it, without the sentence having to settle which.

phrases.translation: for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water;
phrases.ar: وَإِنَّ مِنَ ٱلۡحِجَارَةِ لَمَا يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنۡهُ ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُۚ وَإِنَّ مِنۡهَا لَمَا يَشَّقَّقُ
phrases.explanation:
The three kinds of stone are then explained, since they are what the comparison rests on. The first is the stone from which rivers gush forth, and the verb used is traced to its form, which is built from the saying that the water gushed forth, meaning that it comes out in quantity and with force.

The second is the stone that splits open so that water comes out of it, and it is explained as a stone that cracks and releases what is in it, which is less than the gushing of the first kind but is still water leaving a stone.

The point of naming them is that stones are not all alike in what they give. Some pour out rivers, some release water when they split, so a heart that is harder than these is being compared to things that do yield something, and the comparison is meant to make the hardness look worse rather than merely great.

phrases.translation: while others are humbled in awe of Allah.
phrases.ar: فَيَخۡرُجُ مِنۡهُ ٱلۡمَآءُۚ وَإِنَّ مِنۡهَا لَمَا يَهۡبِطُ
phrases.explanation:
The third kind is discussed by the people of interpretation, who disagreed about the meaning of the falling down of those stones. The explanation given is that among stones are some that fall down out of fear of Allah, and the falling is read in the light of that fear rather than as ordinary collapsing.

A note on the wording accompanies it. The letters attached to the word for what are placed there for emphasis of the report, so the sentence asserts the thing rather than leaving it open.

It is then observed that Allah described the stones only with what He described them with here, namely that among them are kinds that gush, that split and that fall, and that in agreement with this the people of interpretation spoke, so the description is not extended beyond what the verse gives.

phrases.translation: And Allah is never unaware of what you do
phrases.ar: مِنۡ خَشۡيَةِ ٱللَّهِۗ وَمَا ٱللَّهُ بِغَٰفِلٍ عَمَّا تَعۡمَلُونَ
phrases.explanation: The closing clause is explained as an address to the community spoken to. Allah is not unmindful of what they do, and the sense given is that nothing of their conduct is hidden from Him. It is placed after the description of their hearts because a hardening that no one else can see is still known, and the verse ends by saying so.

phrases.translation: Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you,
phrases.ar: أَفَتَطۡمَعُونَ أَن يُؤۡمِنُواْ لَكُمۡ وَقَدۡ
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained as addressed to the Companions of the Prophet. By do you then desire, Allah is speaking to them about their hope concerning these people, and the thing hoped for is explained next.

That they should believe you means that they should affirm the believers as truthful in what their Prophet brought them, so the belief spoken of is belief directed at people and not only at a message. The question therefore asks whether a group described in the rest of the verse can be expected to give that kind of belief.

phrases.translation: though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it
phrases.ar: كَانَ فَرِيقٞ مِّنۡهُمۡ يَسۡمَعُونَ كَلَٰمَ ٱللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُحَرِّفُونَهُۥ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا عَقَلُوهُ وَهُمۡ يَعۡلَمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The group named within them is then identified, and two interpretations of the clause are recorded. The correct one, and the one that most accords with what the outward wording of the recitation indicates, is what al-Rabi ibn Anas said and what Ibn Ishaq transmitted from some of the scholars.

On that reading Allah meant by it only those of the children of Israel who heard His word, just as Moses heard it from Him, and then distorted and altered it after they had heard it, understood it and comprehended it. The reason given for this reading is that Allah reported the distortion as coming from a party of them who heard the word of Allah, so the party described is one that heard the word itself and not one that received it second hand. Their alteration is therefore stated to happen after understanding, which is what makes it knowing.

phrases.translation: When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.”
phrases.ar: وَإِذَا لَقُواْ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ قَالُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا
phrases.explanation: The verse is explained as an announcement from Allah about the people it describes, reporting what they say when they meet those who believe. A further saying is transmitted from Ibn Abbas about its explanation, and other accounts are recorded beside it, so the words are read both as a report of a habit and as a description of a particular group among them.

phrases.translation: But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you,
phrases.ar: وَإِذَا خَلَا بَعۡضُهُمۡ إِلَىٰ بَعۡضٖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتُحَدِّثُونَهُم بِمَا
phrases.explanation:
Being alone with one another is explained as what happens when some of these Jews, whose character the verse describes, withdraw together and speak among themselves. The thing they speak about is then discussed, and the exegetes differed concerning the explanation of the words what Allah has revealed to you, with several answers recorded one after the other.

Since the meaning of the word translated as disclose is as described earlier, the sense of their saying becomes clear, and the reproach is understood as being about handing something over to the believers.

phrases.translation: so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”
phrases.ar: فَتَحَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ لِيُحَآجُّوكُم بِهِۦ عِندَ رَبِّكُمۡۚ أَفَلَا تَعۡقِلُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The explanation preferred for the verse is then given, and it is the saying of those who read the reproach as being about disclosing to the believers what their own books contain, since that is what the believers would use to argue against them before their Lord. Because that is so, it is necessary that their mutual reproaches, which took place among them, pertained to that matter and not to something else.

The closing question is discussed last. Do you not understand is explained as an announcement from Allah concerning the people who were reproaching one another, so the words stand as His description of what they said to each other when they were alone.

phrases.translation: Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal
phrases.ar: أَوَلَا يَعۡلَمُونَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَعۡلَمُ مَا يُسِرُّونَ وَمَا يُعۡلِنُونَ
phrases.explanation: The question is explained by naming the people it concerns. It is addressed to those among the Jews who reproach their brethren for saying we believe when they meet the believers, and for telling the believers what is in their books concerning the description of the Messenger and his mission. What they conceal is what they keep hidden from the believers, and what they make public is what they say in front of them, and both are known to Allah.

phrases.translation: And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies,
phrases.ar: وَمِنۡهُمۡ أُمِّيُّونَ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ إِلَّآ أَمَانِيَّ
phrases.explanation:
The group described is identified first. Among them are unlettered ones, and the word is explained as naming those who neither write nor read. Another explanation of it is recorded and then set aside, on the ground that it goes against what is known from the widespread language of the Arabs, so the plain sense of the word is kept.

What they do not know is then explained. They do not know the Book means that they do not know what is in the Book that Allah sent down, which is a stronger statement than not being able to read it, since it concerns its contents.

The exception that follows is treated as a matter of grammar. With the word for except, what comes after it is excepted from the meaning of what comes before it and from its description, even where each of the two is of a different nature and kind from the other. Some grammarians call this a disjoined exception, on account of the expression after the word being disjoined from the meaning of what stands before it. The test given for it is that this is the case everywhere it is appropriate to put the word but in place of except, because then one knows that the second meaning is disjoined from the first, and the sentence about unlettered people who do not know the Book is offered as the example.

What indicates the correctness of this explanation, and shows that it is more fitting than the other sayings, is the clause that closes the verse. Allah informs about them that they wish what they wish of lies out of conjecture on their part and not out of certainty. If the meaning were that they recite the Book, they would not be conjecturers, and the same follows if the meaning were that they desire it, because a person who recites a thing knows it when he reflects on it, and it is not appropriate to describe such a person as only conjecturing.

phrases.translation: and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate
phrases.ar: وَإِنۡ هُمۡ إِلَّا يَظُنُّونَ
phrases.explanation:
The last clause is explained as a statement about their state of mind. They do nothing but conjecture, and the meaning given for the exception is that they doubt and do not know, so what is denied to them is knowledge and what is left with them is guesswork.

The verse is then summed up as a whole. Among them is one who does not write, does not trace letters, does not know the Book, and has nothing but wishes of lies and conjecture. The description divides the people spoken of, since the group named here has no hold on the text at all, and the verses before it concerned people who heard the word of Allah and altered it after understanding.

phrases.translation: So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain!
phrases.ar: فَوَيۡلٞ لِّلَّذِينَ يَكۡتُبُونَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ بِأَيۡدِيهِمۡ ثُمَّ يَقُولُونَ هَٰذَا مِنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ لِيَشۡتَرُواْ بِهِۦ ثَمَنٗا قَلِيلٗاۖ
phrases.explanation:
A question is raised about the mention of the hands. Writing among human beings happens with the hand in any case, so what does adding it here mean? The answer given is that the phrase points to the people doing it themselves, so the writing is theirs and not something they inherited or copied.

Those meant by it are then identified as the people who distorted the Book of Allah among the Jews of the children of Israel, who wrote something with their own hands and then said this is from Allah, in order to sell it for a small price.

phrases.translation: So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned
phrases.ar: فَوَيۡلٞ لَّهُم مِّمَّا كَتَبَتۡ أَيۡدِيهِمۡ وَوَيۡلٞ لَّهُم مِّمَّا يَكۡسِبُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Two woes are then named, one for what their hands wrote and one for what they earn. The first is explained as concerning that which their hands wrote of what is not in the Book of Allah, so the wrong lies in the writing itself and not only in the claim made about it.

The second is explained as concerning what they gain by it, which is the price they take from people who accept the writing as revelation. The doubling of the woe is therefore not a repetition but a division, one for the act of putting words into the Book and one for living on what those words bring in.

phrases.translation: ˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”
phrases.ar: وَقَالُواْ لَن تَمَسَّنَا ٱلنَّارُ إِلَّآ أَيَّامٗا مَّعۡدُودَةٗۚ قُلۡ أَتَّخَذۡتُمۡ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ عَهۡدٗا فَلَن يُخۡلِفَ ٱللَّهُ عَهۡدَهُۥٓۖ أَمۡ تَقُولُونَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
What the Jews said is explained first. By their words they meant that the Fire will not touch their bodies and that they will not enter it, except for a number of days. The days are called counted even though their number is not given in the revelation, and the reason for that wording is discussed, since Allah reported their saying in the form they used it.

The answer they are given is then explained. When they said this, Allah told His Prophet to say to the community of the Jews, have you taken a covenant with Allah, that is, have you received from Him a firm promise that He will not put you in the Fire beyond those days, or are you saying about Allah what you do not know. The two alternatives leave nothing between them, since a claim about the hereafter either rests on a promise from Allah or on nothing.

The reports from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada about the days they meant are judged to be in accordance with this reading. Among what Allah granted His servants of His firm promise is that whoever believes in Him and obeys His command He will deliver on the Day of Resurrection from His Fire.

phrases.translation: But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin
phrases.ar: بَلَىٰۚ مَن كَسَبَ سَيِّئَةٗ وَأَحَٰطَتۡ بِهِۦ خَطِيٓـَٔتُهُۥ
phrases.explanation:
The opening word is treated first as a matter of language. The particle translated as but no is an affirmation that follows a statement beginning with a negation, so it turns back what was just denied and asserts the opposite of it. Here it answers the claim that the Fire will touch them only for a number of days.

The sentence that follows is then explained as a refutation by Allah of those who made that claim, and its shape is general rather than aimed at one group. Whoever earns an evil deed and is encompassed by his sin is named without restricting the description to the Jews, which is what makes it an answer to them.

The evil deed mentioned in this place is then identified. It is ascribing partners to Allah, and the reasoning for taking it that way is set out at length, since the verse goes on to promise its people an unending stay in the Fire and that promise does not fit a sin short of disbelief. The explanation is therefore fixed by the consequence attached to it.

A supposition is examined along the way. If someone holds that those among the believers to whom eternal abiding in the Garden is due are only some of them, the discussion that follows bears on who abides forever and who does not, and on the difference between a sin that surrounds a person and a sin that does not. The point of raising it is that the eternity named in the verse is tied to the kind of deed described, not to every wrongdoing a believer commits.

phrases.translation: will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever
phrases.ar: فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ أَصۡحَٰبُ ٱلنَّارِۖ هُمۡ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The people named are then explained. The inhabitants of the Fire means the people of the Fire, and the words they therein are explained as their abiding forever in it. The last word is given its sense of remaining without an end, so the verse states both belonging and duration.

It is this duration that answers the claim in the verse before it, since a number of days and an unending stay cannot both be true of the same people.

phrases.translation: And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever
phrases.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ أَصۡحَٰبُ ٱلۡجَنَّةِۖ هُمۡ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Those who believe are explained as those who held to be true what the Messenger of Allah brought them, and their righteous deeds are joined to that belief as the second condition of the promise.

This verse and the one before it are then read together as an announcement from Allah to His servants concerning the lasting nature of the two states, so the pair is not a description of two groups only but a statement that what each group enters does not end.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ أَخَذۡنَا مِيثَٰقَ بَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ
phrases.explanation: The covenant is named first, and the word for it was already demonstrated earlier in the work, being derived from the word for a surety. What is meant here is the covenant Allah took from the children of Israel, and the verses that follow list what it required of them.

phrases.translation: ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah;
phrases.ar: لَا تَعۡبُدُونَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهَ
phrases.explanation:
The first requirement is the worship of Allah alone, and the recitation of the verb that carries it is discussed at length. The reciters differ over it, some reciting it with the letter that addresses the people directly and some with the letter that reports about them, and the two readings give the clause two shapes, one a command spoken to them and one a statement of what they were bound to.

A point of grammar accompanies the difference. The particle that would ordinarily introduce the clause is omitted, and the omission is explained, since the sense is complete without it and the verb stands in a form that shows what was left out. A parallel is quoted in which a verb is placed in the nominative even though it would have suited the construction to introduce it with that particle.

The meaning of the covenant as a whole is then given in one sentence. Allah made the covenant with the children of Israel that they would worship none but Him, and be good to their parents, and the rest of the list that the verse goes on to name.

phrases.translation: be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy;
phrases.ar: وَبِٱلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ إِحۡسَانٗا وَذِي ٱلۡقُرۡبَىٰ وَٱلۡيَتَٰمَىٰ وَٱلۡمَسَٰكِينِ
phrases.explanation:
Kindness to parents is followed by three further groups, and each word is explained. The near kinsman is described as the one whose ties they were required to maintain, and the word for kinship is traced to its form, a verbal noun on a known pattern derived from the saying that a person's womb drew near to mine, so the word itself carries the idea of nearness of birth.

The needy is then explained as the one who shows himself submissive and abased on account of poverty and want, and the form of the word is given with it. A point of grammar covers the construction, since the word for goodness stands in the accusative on account of a verb understood but not spoken, whose meaning is conveyed by the words before it.

phrases.translation: speak kindly to people;
phrases.ar: وَقُولُواْ لِلنَّاسِ حُسۡنٗا
phrases.explanation:
Speaking well to people is discussed first in its recitation. The word for good is read in more than one way, and most of the reciters of Kufa, with one exception, read it in a particular form. A claim about the meaning of one of those forms is examined and rejected, and the recitation that takes a different shape altogether is judged to contradict the recitation transmitted by the others, so the reading preferred is the one the copies agree on.

The good speech commanded is then explained. It concerns the speech those of the children of Israel whose case is described here were required to use toward people, and the explanation given is the one that fits the command as it stands in the covenant.

phrases.translation: establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.”
phrases.ar: وَأَقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُواْ
phrases.explanation:
Establishing the prayer is explained as performing it with the rights that the person praying is obliged to give it, so the word concerns more than going through the movements.

The alms tax follows, and its meaning and origin were set out earlier in the work, so they are not repeated here. The two requirements are named together, as they are in the other places where this covenant is listed.

phrases.translation: But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent
phrases.ar: ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ ثُمَّ تَوَلَّيۡتُمۡ إِلَّا قَلِيلٗا مِّنكُمۡ وَأَنتُم مُّعۡرِضُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The turning away is then explained as a report from Allah about the Jews of the children of Israel, that they turned back from what the covenant required, with the exception of a few of them.

The closing words are discussed next. Some said that Allah meant by them the Jews who lived in the time of the Prophet, so the aversion named is that of people who were still alive when the verse came down. Others said that the sentence is an address directed to those present about what their predecessors did, and both readings are recorded.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes,
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ أَخَذۡنَا مِيثَٰقَكُمۡ لَا تَسۡفِكُونَ دِمَآءَكُمۡ وَلَا تُخۡرِجُونَ أَنفُسَكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِكُمۡ
phrases.explanation:
The covenant taken here is a second one, and its content is explained. The shedding of blood means the pouring out of blood and causing it to flow, and the prohibition concerns the blood of one another, so it binds each of them toward the rest of his own people.

It is also noted as permissible that the meaning of the prohibition is wider than the act itself, namely that a man assists in the shedding of another's blood, since helping to bring it about falls under the same prohibition. In accordance with this explanation the people of interpretation spoke, and the reports naming them are given.

The second half of the covenant is the prohibition on expelling one another from their homes, which is joined to the first because both concern the safety of a person among his own people.

phrases.translation: you gave your pledge and bore witness
phrases.ar: ثُمَّ أَقۡرَرۡتُمۡ وَأَنتُمۡ تَشۡهَدُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Affirming is then explained. By the words then you affirmed, Allah means the covenant that He took from them, namely that they would not shed one another's blood nor expel one another from their homes, so what they affirmed is the same thing the verse has just described.

The words while you bear witness are discussed next. The people of interpretation differed concerning who is addressed by them. Some took the address as running to those present, and others said that the verse is an announcement by Allah about their predecessors, with the address turned toward the descendants because they hold to what those predecessors accepted. Both readings are recorded, and each is explained.

phrases.translation: But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression;
phrases.ar: ثُمَّ أَنتُمۡ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ تَقۡتُلُونَ أَنفُسَكُمۡ وَتُخۡرِجُونَ فَرِيقٗا مِّنكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِهِمۡ تَظَٰهَرُونَ عَلَيۡهِم بِٱلۡإِثۡمِ
phrases.explanation:
The opening words are explained, and two interpretations of them are possible. On the first, the phrase points at the people addressed as they now stand, so the sense is here you are, doing this after affirming that covenant. On the other interpretation the meaning is that they are a people who kill one another, which returns the description to what they are rather than to where they are.

The words for their mutual aid are then explained. Mutual assistance is the same as supporting one another, and it is called by that name on account of the way one person's back is put behind another's, so the word carries the idea of people lending each other force. The enmity named with it is explained from its form as well, being a pattern built from the word for transgression, and the ordinary use of the verb is quoted.

The conduct described is then placed. An account was related concerning this behavior of theirs with the two tribes among whom they lived, so the verse is read as describing something that was still happening when it came down and not only something their ancestors had done.

phrases.translation: and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?
phrases.ar: وَٱلۡعُدۡوَٰنِ وَإِن يَأۡتُوكُمۡ أُسَٰرَىٰ تُفَٰدُوهُمۡ وَهُوَ مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيۡكُمۡ إِخۡرَاجُهُمۡۚ أَفَتُؤۡمِنُونَ بِبَعۡضِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ وَتَكۡفُرُونَ بِبَعۡضٖۚ
phrases.explanation:
The reproach that follows is explained at length. If those expelled come to them as captives they ransom them, while the expelling of them was forbidden to them by the same covenant, so the verse holds two parts of one agreement side by side and shows them keeping one and breaking the other.

The word for captives is discussed in the recitation. The reciters differed concerning how it is read, and the explanation of each reading is given. Whoever recited it in one of the two forms meant the plural of the word for a captive, since it is built on a pattern that carries that plural, and some claimed that the two forms differ in meaning, with one naming captives in a particular state and the other naming them generally. The reports of who held each view are given with them.

The question that closes the verse is then explained. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part is put to people who acted on the clause about ransoming captives while ignoring the clause about expelling them, so belief in part of the Book is shown by what they did and rejection of the rest by what they left undone.

phrases.translation: Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life
phrases.ar: فَمَا جَزَآءُ مَن يَفۡعَلُ ذَٰلِكَ مِنكُمۡ إِلَّا خِزۡيٞ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ
phrases.explanation:
The recompense is then stated and explained. What is the recompense of whoever does that among them except disgrace in the life of this world, and the explanation of the word for recompense is given with it.

The disgrace itself is discussed, and the reports differ about what it was. Some said it is the levying of the tax from them for as long as they remain under the rule of the believers, and others said that the disgrace with which they were recompensed in the worldly life was the driving out of them by the Messenger of Allah. Both accounts are recorded, and each is explained as a fulfillment of the verse in this world before the next.

phrases.translation: and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment?
phrases.ar: وَيَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ يُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰٓ أَشَدِّ ٱلۡعَذَابِۗ
phrases.explanation:
The punishment of the next world is then explained. On the Day of Resurrection they are returned to the severest punishment, and the recitation of the verb is discussed, the reading preferred of the two being the one in conformity with what precedes it.

A claim about the meaning is examined and set aside. Some said that they are returned to something severer than what they were in, but the statement of whoever says that is judged to have no valid meaning, because Allah informs in this verse of what awaits them on that day rather than comparing two punishments with each other.

phrases.translation: For Allah is never unaware of what you do
phrases.ar: وَمَا ٱللَّهُ بِغَٰفِلٍ عَمَّا تَعۡمَلُونَ
phrases.explanation: The verse closes by stating that Allah is not unaware of what they do. The clause is attached to the two punishments named before it, one in this world and one on the Day of Resurrection, and it is the reason both can be promised with certainty, since nothing of the conduct described is hidden from the One who repays it.

phrases.translation: These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped
phrases.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱشۡتَرَوُاْ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنۡيَا بِٱلۡأٓخِرَةِۖ فَلَا يُخَفَّفُ عَنۡهُمُ ٱلۡعَذَابُ وَلَا هُمۡ يُنصَرُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The people named are identified as those of whom Allah informed that they believe in part of the Book and reject part of it, so this verse continues the description of the same group rather than introducing a new one.

The buying described is then explained. Since they sold their share in the felicity of the hereafter for the life of this world, Allah informed that the punishment will not be lightened for them. The last clause is explained as a statement that no one will help them in the hereafter, so neither is the punishment reduced nor is anyone found to prevent it, and the two denials cover the only two ways a punishment ends.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers.
phrases.ar: وَلَقَدۡ ءَاتَيۡنَا مُوسَى ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَقَفَّيۡنَا مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦ بِٱلرُّسُلِۖ
phrases.explanation:
Giving the Book is explained first as sending it down to Moses, since that is what the verb means here.

The word translated as sent after him in succession is then explained. It means that Allah caused them to follow one another and to come after one another, and the same verb is used in ordinary speech of people or things following in a line, so the image is one of a queue rather than of a single replacement.

The messengers named are identified as the prophets, and the word is given as the plural of the word for one sent, with the ordinary forms of that word quoted. What is meant by the clause is then stated in full, that Allah caused the messengers to come one after another to them after Moses, which is why the verse can speak of a long history of revelation rather than of one book and one prophet. A line of poetry is quoted for the use of the verb, with a note on who it is correctly attributed to.

phrases.translation: And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit.
phrases.ar: وَءَاتَيۡنَا عِيسَى ٱبۡنَ مَرۡيَمَ ٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتِ
phrases.explanation:
The clear proofs given to Jesus are explained as the proofs and indications of his prophethood. Strengthening him is then explained as giving him strength and helping him.

The spirit of holiness is discussed, and the explanations recorded include that it is the Gospel and that it is the name by which Jesus raised the dead to life. The correct explanation is the saying of those who took it to be Jibril, since Allah reported that He strengthened Jesus with it. Jibril is called a spirit and attached to holiness because he was made by Allah's creating into a spirit from Him without birth from a father.

phrases.translation: Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others
phrases.ar: وَأَيَّدۡنَٰهُ بِرُوحِ ٱلۡقُدُسِۗ أَفَكُلَّمَا جَآءَكُمۡ رَسُولُۢ بِمَا لَا تَهۡوَىٰٓ أَنفُسُكُمُ ٱسۡتَكۡبَرۡتُمۡ فَفَرِيقٗا كَذَّبۡتُمۡ وَفَرِيقٗا تَقۡتُلُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is then summed up as a single address. Allah says to them, O community of the Jews of the children of Israel, We gave Moses the Torah, We caused the messengers to follow one after another after him, We gave Jesus the son of Mary the clear proofs and strengthened him with the spirit of holiness, and then whenever a messenger came to you with something your souls did not like, you acted arrogantly, denying a party and killing a party.

The shape of the sentence is what carries the rebuke. The gifts are listed first, so the people addressed are reminded that revelation reached them repeatedly and in more than one form, through a book, through a succession of messengers, and through signs given to one messenger in particular. What follows that list is therefore not a single failure but a habit, and the verse describes it as happening every time a messenger came.

Two outcomes are named rather than one. A party of the messengers they denied and a party they killed, so the response described runs from refusal to violence. The clause about what their souls disliked gives the reason attached to both, and it locates the objection not in the standing of the messenger but in what he brought, which is why the answer to it is described as arrogance.

phrases.translation: They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”
phrases.ar: وَقَالُواْ قُلُوبُنَا غُلۡفُۢۚ
phrases.explanation:
What they say about their hearts is discussed in the recitation first. The reciters differ over the reading of the word, some reading it in a form that means the hearts are within coverings, and others reading it with a different vocalization that they explained in another way. The reports naming who read each are given.

The reading that is alone permissible is then stated, and it is the one with a particular vowel pattern, on the ground that what the proof is unanimous about constitutes a binding proof for whoever it reaches, a principle demonstrated earlier. The sense of the saying is that they claimed their hearts were wrapped so that nothing said to them could get in.

phrases.translation: In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief.
phrases.ar: بَل لَّعَنَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُفۡرِهِمۡ
phrases.explanation:
The answer to that claim is explained. By the words but Allah cursed them, Allah means that He rejected and banished them on account of their disbelief, so the covering they claimed is turned into the thing done to them.

The word for curse is then traced to its origin, which is driving away, removal and rejection, and the ordinary saying built on it is quoted, that Allah cursed such a one, meaning He removed and drove him away. In this sentence lies a refutation of their claim, since a heart rejected by Allah is not one that cannot receive anything but one that has been shut by its own disbelief.

phrases.translation: They have but little faith
phrases.ar: فَقَلِيلٗا مَّا يُؤۡمِنُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The closing words are explained, and the exegetes differ over them. Some took them one way, and others said that the meaning is that they believe only in a small portion of what they hold in their hands, so what is described as little is their belief rather than their number.

A point of language accompanies the discussion. The particle attached to the word for little is examined, and a witness is quoted from poetry in which the same particle is treated as redundant, with the meaning of the line given alongside it.

phrases.translation: Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists,
phrases.ar: وَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمۡ كِتَٰبٞ مِّنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ مُصَدِّقٞ لِّمَا مَعَهُمۡ
phrases.explanation: Praying for victory is explained as what they used to do before this. They asked to be given the upper hand over those who disbelieved, and the asking is described as something they were in the habit of, so the verse recalls a practice of theirs rather than a single request. The explanation of the clause is then given in full, together with what they were asking by, since their prayer for victory was tied to a prophet whose coming they expected.

phrases.translation: when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it.
phrases.ar: وَكَانُواْ مِن قَبۡلُ يَسۡتَفۡتِحُونَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ فَلَمَّا جَآءَهُم مَّا عَرَفُواْ كَفَرُواْ بِهِۦۚ
phrases.explanation:
The coming of the Book is then explained. A Book from Allah came to them confirming what was already with them, and the sense given is that they recognized it, so the rejection described is not of something unfamiliar.

A question of grammar is raised about the sentence. Where is the main clause answering the words when there came to them? One answer is that the answer lies contained in the particle that follows, so the clause about their rejecting it completes the sentence.

phrases.translation: So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers
phrases.ar: فَلَعۡنَةُ ٱللَّهِ عَلَى ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The curse is explained by referring back to what was already demonstrated earlier about the meaning of the word, so it is not set out again here.

The meaning of the verse is then given. So the abasement and banishment of Allah is upon those who deny what they have been given, and the curse is attached to disbelief in particular, which is the same thing the verse has just described them as doing when they recognized the Book and rejected it.

phrases.translation: Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—
phrases.ar: بِئۡسَمَا ٱشۡتَرَوۡاْ بِهِۦٓ أَنفُسَهُمۡ أَن
phrases.explanation:
The exclamation is explained from its root. The word translated as miserable comes from a verb meaning to be in misery and wretchedness, and the form is discussed, its first letter being made quiescent after a particular vowel, with the ordinary shape of the verb given. It is also possible that the word belongs to the usage of those who transfer a vowel from one letter to another, and that account is recorded beside the first.

The particle joined to it is then examined by the grammarians, who differed about it. Some of the grammarians of Basra took it in one way, and others said that the two words form a single whole which places what follows it in the nominative, as transmitted from one of the scholars of the language. The Arabs are then quoted using the construction, in a saying about a wretched marriage with no dowry, where the particle is made to carry the whole exclamation.

The reason named in the verse is explained last. The word translated as resenting means out of transgression and envy, so the disbelief described is given a motive rather than being left as bare rejection. The meaning of the verse as a whole is then stated. Wretched is the matter for which they sold their souls, namely their disbelief in what Allah sent down, carried out out of resentment that Allah should send it down at all.

phrases.translation: denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath.
phrases.ar: يَكۡفُرُواْ بِمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ بَغۡيًا أَن يُنَزِّلَ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضۡلِهِۦ عَلَىٰ مَن يَشَآءُ مِنۡ عِبَادِهِۦۖ
phrases.explanation:
What is resented is then named. That Allah sends down of His grace on whom He wills of His servants is a clause whose explanation and meaning were already given earlier, and it is mentioned again here to complete the sense of the verse, since the grace resented is the revelation given to someone other than themselves.

The result of their choice is then explained. They returned with wrath upon wrath, and the sense of returning with a thing is that they came back carrying it. The doubling is explained at length, and the meaning of the wrath of Allah toward those of His creatures on whom He is wrathful was already set out earlier, so it is not repeated, but the two wraths are distinguished from one another.

phrases.translation: And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment
phrases.ar: فَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٍ عَلَىٰ غَضَبٖۚ وَلِلۡكَٰفِرِينَ عَذَابٞ مُّهِينٞ
phrases.explanation:
The punishment named at the end is explained as one that humiliates. For the disbelievers there is a humiliating punishment, and the explanation given concerns both parts of the description, the punishment itself and the abasement attached to it, so what is promised is not only pain but a pain that puts the person beneath others.

The verse ends on this word because the arrogance described earlier in the passage is answered by it, and the humiliation named here is the counterpart of the disdain with which they met the messengers.

phrases.translation: When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,”
phrases.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمۡ ءَامِنُواْ بِمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ قَالُواْ
phrases.explanation: The exchange is explained as a report of what they say. When it is said to them, believe in what Allah has sent down, they answer that they believe in what was sent down to them, so the command is general and the answer restricts it. The words are addressed to the Jews of the children of Israel, and what they claim is not disbelief but a belief limited to one book.

phrases.translation: they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,”
phrases.ar: نُؤۡمِنُ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ عَلَيۡنَا
phrases.explanation: Rejecting what comes after it is then explained, and the word for after is taken in this place as meaning other than or besides, just as the word is used in ordinary speech in that sense. The rejection is therefore not of a later time only but of anything other than the book they already hold.

phrases.translation: and they deny what came afterwards,
phrases.ar: وَيَكۡفُرُونَ بِمَا وَرَآءَهُۥ
phrases.explanation: The Book they reject is described as the truth confirming what is with them. The explanation given is that what was sent down agrees with the scripture they hold rather than contradicting it, so the confirmation is offered as the reason the rejection makes no sense, since a book that supports what they already accept cannot be dismissed on the ground that it is not theirs.

phrases.translation: though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before,
phrases.ar: وَهُوَ ٱلۡحَقُّ مُصَدِّقٗا لِّمَا مَعَهُمۡۗ قُلۡ فَلِمَ تَقۡتُلُونَ أَنۢبِيَآءَ ٱللَّهِ
phrases.explanation:
The question put to them is then explained. Say, why do you kill the prophets of Allah formerly, is addressed to those among the Jews of the time, and the correct view about the address is given at length, since the killing was done by their forefathers and not by them.

The word formerly is explained as meaning before today, which fixes the question on a past they own rather than on something happening now.

phrases.translation: if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”
phrases.ar: مِن قَبۡلُ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤۡمِنِينَ
phrases.explanation: The condition attached to the question is then explained. By the words if you are believers, Allah means if you believe in what He sent down to you as you claim, so the condition takes their own claim and turns it against them. A people who killed the prophets sent to them are asked how they can be believers in what those prophets brought, and the question is left for them to answer.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully
phrases.ar: وَلَقَدۡ جَآءَكُم مُّوسَىٰ بِٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتِ ثُمَّ ٱتَّخَذۡتُمُ ٱلۡعِجۡلَ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦ وَأَنتُمۡ ظَٰلِمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The coming of Moses is explained first. Verily Moses came to them with the clear proofs, and the meaning of the address is given, that there came to them, O company of the Jews and children of Israel, what is described.

The proofs are then explained as proofs. Allah called them clear proofs because for whoever looked at them they made clear that they were a sign from Allah, so the clarity lies in what the looking produces rather than in the number of signs.

What followed is then explained. After him they took the calf, and the pronoun in after him is discussed, since it can refer back to Moses or to the mention of his coming, and the interpretation is given on each of the two readings. The wrongdoing named at the end of the verse is attached to that taking, so the sequence is a coming with clear proofs followed at once by worship given to something else.

phrases.translation: And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.”
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ أَخَذۡنَا مِيثَٰقَكُمۡ وَرَفَعۡنَا فَوۡقَكُمُ ٱلطُّورَ خُذُواْ مَآ ءَاتَيۡنَٰكُم بِقُوَّةٖ وَٱسۡمَعُواْۖ قَالُواْ سَمِعۡنَا وَعَصَيۡنَا
phrases.explanation:
The covenant is explained as one Allah took from them, and the verse is read as a reminder, remember when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you. What the covenant required is then given, that they hold fast to what Allah gave them with strength and listen.

The two words for hearing and obeying are explained. By hearing is meant accepting what one hears, and by obedience, obedience to what is commanded, so the two together describe a person who takes in a command and then acts on it. A witness from poetry is quoted for the language, with a note on the better reading of the line.

Their answer is then explained. They said we hear and we disobey, which joins the first half of what was required to the refusal of the second, and the verse reports the answer as they gave it rather than correcting it at that point.

phrases.translation: The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”
phrases.ar: وَأُشۡرِبُواْ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ ٱلۡعِجۡلَ بِكُفۡرِهِمۡۚ قُلۡ بِئۡسَمَا يَأۡمُرُكُم بِهِۦٓ إِيمَٰنُكُمۡ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤۡمِنِينَ
phrases.explanation:
What was put into their hearts is explained first. They were made to drink the calf in their hearts by their disbelief, and the exegetes differed concerning it. Some said that what is meant is that the love of the calf was made to enter their hearts, and others said that the meaning is that they were given to drink the water in which the filings of the calf had been scattered, so one reading takes the drinking as an image and the other as an event. The reports naming who said each are given.

The image is then explained from the language. A witness is quoted in which a speaker names a black poison and is content with the mention of the black without mentioning the poison, because the word already carries it, which is the same way of speaking in which a heart is said to be given a thing to drink.

The verse closes with the rebuke they are told to answer. Say, how evil is the thing your belief prompts you to do, if you are believers, which turns their own claim back on them, since a belief that produces the killing of prophets and the worship of a calf is described as no belief at all.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”
phrases.ar: قُلۡ إِن كَانَتۡ لَكُمُ ٱلدَّارُ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَالِصَةٗ مِّن دُونِ ٱلنَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُاْ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained first as a proof. It belongs to the arguments by which Allah furnished His Prophet against the Jews, and its force is set out at length, since it puts a claim of theirs to a test that they cannot take.

The claim is that the home of the hereafter belongs to them alone with Allah, apart from the rest of people. The answer to it is a challenge rather than a counter argument. If that is so, they are told to wish for death, since a person who is certain that the next world is his alone and that it is better than this one has no reason to hold on to this one.

A report is then given which fixes the outcome. It is reported that the Messenger of Allah said that if the Jews had wished for death they would have died, and that none of them would have been left on the face of the earth. The point drawn from it is that on that day the affair of the Jews became clear even to whoever had been unsure of it, and their lying and their slander were exposed by their silence rather than by a reply.

The exegetes then disagreed about the reason why Allah commanded His Prophet to call the Jews to this, and the explanations recorded are given with the reports naming who held each of them.

phrases.translation: But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers
phrases.ar: وَلَن يَتَمَنَّوۡهُ أَبَدَۢا بِمَا قَدَّمَتۡ أَيۡدِيهِمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
phrases.explanation:
That they will never wish for it is explained as an announcement from Allah concerning the Jews and their aversion to the thing they were challenged to, so the verse states in advance what their answer would be and then reports that they gave it.

The reason attached is then explained. Because of what their hands have sent ahead means because of what their hands have done, and the question is asked why the deed is ascribed to the hand when much of it is done otherwise. The answer given is that this way of speaking is used because the majority of the offenses people commit are committed with the hand, so the hand is named for the whole of the acting.

It is then noted that Allah spoke in this way to the Arabs, using the idiom they already carried, which is why the sentence can name the hands and mean the deeds without being misunderstood by the people who first heard it.

The closing clause is explained last. Allah is all knowing of the wrongdoers, and the sense given is that nothing of what they sent ahead is hidden from Him, so the knowledge named here is what makes their unwillingness to wish for death a confession rather than a mere hesitation.

phrases.translation: You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people,
phrases.ar: وَلَتَجِدَنَّهُمۡ أَحۡرَصَ ٱلنَّاسِ عَلَىٰ حَيَوٰةٖ وَمِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَشۡرَكُواْۚ
phrases.explanation: The description is explained as a report about them. Allah says that the Prophet will find them the most avid of all people for life, and the reason for that description is then given. Allah described the Jews as the people most avid for life only because of the knowledge they carry, since a people who know what awaits them have more reason to hold on to this life than people who do not know it.

phrases.translation: even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years.
phrases.ar: يَوَدُّ أَحَدُهُمۡ لَوۡ يُعَمَّرُ أَلۡفَ سَنَةٖ
phrases.explanation:
The comparison with those who associate partners is then explained. Even more than the polytheists, and the sense given is that the polytheists are described in a report from Allah as people who also long for life, since they have no expectation of anything beyond it, and the Jews are placed above them in avidity. The difference between the two groups is therefore not that one loves life and the other does not, but that the Jews love it more while knowing what they are going toward.

The wish named after that is explained as each of them wishing that he might be given a life of a thousand years, which is a way of stating the length of the longing rather than a limit set on it.

phrases.translation: But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment.
phrases.ar: وَمَا هُوَ بِمُزَحۡزِحِهِۦ مِنَ ٱلۡعَذَابِ أَن يُعَمَّرَۗ
phrases.explanation:
The answer to that wish is then explained. It will not remove him from the punishment that he should be given a long life, and the construction of the sentence is discussed. Others said that this saying amounts to something else, and the most correct of these sayings is judged to be the one in which a pronoun is understood but not spoken, with the reasoning given for preferring it.

Two points of grammar accompany the reading. The particle introducing the clause about living long is said by a group of the people of interpretation to carry a particular sense, and it is placed in the nominative because it is governed by the word for removing him.

The verb translated as remove is then explained from its root. It means to get away to a distance, and the forms of the verb are quoted from ordinary speech, so what is denied is that a long life pushes the punishment away from the person who lives it.

phrases.translation: And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do
phrases.ar: وَٱللَّهُ بَصِيرُۢ بِمَا يَعۡمَلُونَ
phrases.explanation: The closing clause is explained as a statement that Allah sees what they do. The word for seeing is then examined from its form. Its root is a word meaning one who sees, built from the saying I saw so I am one who sees, but the form used here differs from it, and the discussion of that difference is given, so the name describes a seeing that is not limited to what the eye takes in.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know
phrases.ar: قُلۡ مَن كَانَ عَدُوّٗا لِّـجِبۡرِيلَ فَإِنَّهُۥ
phrases.explanation:
The scholars of interpretation are all agreed that this verse was revealed as a response to something said to the Prophet, and the occasion is reported in more than one form. On one account it answers a statement made by some of the Jews about Jibril, and on another the occasion was a dispute that took place between Umar and some of them, and the reports naming who transmitted each account are given.

The explanation of the verse is then set out at length. Whoever is an enemy of Jibril is told that Jibril is the one who sent the Quran down upon the heart of the Prophet by the permission of Allah, so the enmity is aimed at the one who carried the message rather than at the message itself, and the verse answers it by naming what he carried and how.

The mention of the heart is part of that answer, since the sending down is described as reaching the heart of the Prophet, which is the place of understanding and of holding what is given, and the permission of Allah is named with it so that the act is placed under His authority and not under the angel's own choice.

phrases.translation: that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—
phrases.ar: نَزَّلَهُۥ عَلَىٰ قَلۡبِكَ بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِ مُصَدِّقٗا لِّمَا بَيۡنَ يَدَيۡهِ
phrases.explanation:
Confirming what was before it is then explained. What is meant is that the Quran confirms the scriptures that came before it, and the form of the word is given with its grammatical place in the sentence.

The meaning of the clause as a whole is stated, that Jibril sent the Quran down upon the heart of Muhammad confirming what was before it, so the confirmation is offered as a reason why hostility toward the one who brought it makes no sense, since what he brought agrees with what the people hostile to him already hold.

phrases.translation: a guide and good news for the believers.”
phrases.ar: وَهُدٗى وَبُشۡرَىٰ لِلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
phrases.explanation:
Guidance is explained as an indication and a proof, so the word covers both the showing of the way and the evidence that supports it. The glad tiding is then explained as the glad announcement, and what Allah announces by it to the believers is set out.

The two are joined to the believers in particular, and the clause is read as the completion of the description of what Jibril brought down, so the verse ends by naming who benefits from it.

phrases.translation: Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers
phrases.ar: مَن كَانَ عَدُوّٗا لِّلَّهِ وَمَلَٰٓئِكَتِهِۦ وَرُسُلِهِۦ وَجِبۡرِيلَ وَمِيكَىٰلَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَدُوّٞ لِّلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as an announcement from Allah. Whoever is an enemy of Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mikal, then Allah is an enemy of the disbelievers, and the announcement is general, so the enmity named in the answer covers more than the single angel the verse began with.

The occasion is then confirmed by a narration, which indicates that Allah revealed this verse as a rebuke to the Jews because of their disbelief, and the rebuke is answered by widening the sentence rather than by repeating it.

A question is raised about the wording. If the angels have already been named, what is the meaning of repeating the mention of the two of them by their own names? The answer is given at length. The meaning of mentioning the two separately is that when the Jews said that Jibril was their enemy, the two were named so that the hostility they had expressed toward one of them is shown to reach both, and so that the answer given to them covers the angel they named and the angel they did not.

A claim about the construction is examined as well. It was claimed that this is an explicit mention of a name whose part had already been indicated by allusion to it, and that claim is answered, with the reasoning given for the reading preferred.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious
phrases.ar: وَلَقَدۡ أَنزَلۡنَآ إِلَيۡكَ ءَايَٰتِۭ بَيِّنَٰتٖۖ وَمَا يَكۡفُرُ بِهَآ إِلَّا ٱلۡفَٰسِقُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained in two parts. What is meant by the clear revelations sent down to the Prophet is given, and the purport of the verse is then stated as a whole, that Allah sent down to him, in what He revealed to him of the Book, signs that are clear in themselves and do not need something else to make them plain.

The second half is explained as a description of the people who reject them. None rejects them except the perverse means that none denies them, and the word for the perverse is then explained, so the denial described is not the doubt of a person weighing evidence but the refusal of someone who has left the right course.

phrases.translation: Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe
